newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban concede reverses, vow counter-attack.
newsitem.headline: Taleban concede reverses, vow counter-attack.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban government said for the first time on Monday its forces had been pushed back from its front line but vowed it would soon recover towns lost on the plains north of the capital Kabul.
It also said it may be facing the prospect of an Iran-backed uprising on its western border.

The country's 17-day old purist Islamic government lost two key towns in weekend fighting, according to aid sources, and was battling to defend a key airbase and roads 30 minutes' drive north of Kabul, reliable sources said.

Acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Stanakzai said Taleban forces had been ousted from the front-line town of Jabal os-Siraj and were resisting attacks from former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood around Bagram airbase.
"Jabal os-Siraj at the moment is with them, but Bagram airbase is with Taleban and even our forces are ahead of Bagram airbase as well," he told a news conference.
The Taleban, who swept into Kabul in late September, have been reluctant to admit a string of military reverses in the past few days and have accused foreign media of fabricating reports.

Less than a week after being besieged in his Panjsher Valley stronghold a two-hour drive north of Kabul, and apparently fighting to survive, Masood has pushed the Taleban much of the way back to Kabul.
Witnesses said Bagram airbase appeared to be deserted on Monday with Masood forces occupying an area to the east of the base. Two Taleban tanks controlled the road west of the base.
Journalists said all traffic was barred from using the road out of Kabul that runs past the airbase.

While conceding the loss of Jabal os-Siraj and much of Charikar, a town further south along the same road, Stanakzai dismissed the reverses as temporary and said the Taleban would soon counter-attack and resume their assault on the Panjsher.

"Some of their elements have created problems at the backside, so now we have decided to clear our rear. After that we will go ahead and Panjsher valley will not be that difficult for us because now Masood is already finished," he said.

Afghan-watchers doubted it would be so easy. They said Masood appeared to have been successful in mobilising local commanders throughout the plains north of Kabul, inflicting heavy casualties on Taleban forces unused to such tactics.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted witnesses in the eastern city of Jalalabad as saying on Monday that many Taleban casualties had been ferried there.
Stanakzai admitted the Taleban had suffered casualties in the worst fighting the movement had encountered in its sweep of much of the country, but said he did not have figures.
He said some of the wounded were being transferred from Kabul to the southern city of Kandahar, partly to use better facilities and also to make room for more casualties.

"We do not have the same facilities here in Kabul especially in the military hospital, and moreover there were those casualties who had been treated here for one or two days so we wanted to vacate this hospital for more people if they are coming because the battle is going on," he said.
The Taleban militia was preparing the defence of Kabul on Monday, reinforcing positions on the two roads north of the capital and one entering the city from the west.
Stanakzai said the Taleban were confident Masood's forces could not take the capital but were taking no chances.
"I am quite sure they do not have the capability and the capacity to come back to Kabul. For the past two weeks they have been trying but still they have not been able.
"And we have already strengthened our positions in the front line and also we have taken proper measures and precautions around Kabul," he said.

He dismissed reports of an uprising in the western city of Herat, but said that pro-Masood elements in the country's western region appeared to be preparing to cause what he called provocations against the Taleban authorities there.

"Those people who had escaped to the Iran side, according to our reports, want to create some problems on the border, but we are fully aware of the situation and we have answered them in the past also and after this I am hopeful they cannot do anything," he said.
